title: Could tensions 'escalate' before the escalator was invented?

entries.note: From Old English [[from:hwēol]], once pronounced with a hw sound, from Proto-Indo-European [[from:kʷekʷlo-]], also the source of [[same-root:circle]]; the wheel's spread explains such cognates across Europe.
Comes from the same Proto-Indo-European root, [[from:kʷekʷlo-]], as [[same-root:wheel]], so the two words are related despite looking totally different.
Another word from the same root as [[same-root:wheel]] and [[same-root:circle]].
The Greek word comes from the same Proto-Indo-European term as [[same-root:wheel]], a link the hosts credit to the wheel spreading Indo-European speakers.
Its agri- comes from a word for field, shared with [[same-root:acre]], and its culture is that of [[same-root:culture]]; the Old English word was [[see:earth tilth]].
The Old English word for [[see:agriculture]], meaning earth tilling, the turning over of the soil.
Originally not the tool but a unit of land a yoke of oxen could plow in a day, the same meaning as [[see:acre]]; the tool was the [[see:sulh]].
Meant the land a yoke of oxen could plow in a day, like [[see:plow]]; related to the agri- of [[same-root:agriculture]], from a word for field.
The Old English word for the plowing tool, perhaps introduced by the Romans, from Latin [[from?:sulcus]], furrow.
From Latin [[from:colere]], to tend, guard or till, as in [[same-root:cultivating]]; related to [[same-root:colony]]; its figurative sense arose in the 1500s; shares a root with [[same-root:wheel]].
Cultivating land or the mind uses the same sense of tending found in [[same-root:culture]].
Closely related to [[same-root:culture]], originally land tended by farmers or settlers, such as a [[from:colonus]], a tenant farmer settling new lands around Rome.
Praised by the hosts as a terribly satisfying word, fun to say and good for naming a creature.
Probably brought into English by the Romans, from Latin [[from:molere]], to grind, and related to [[same-root:molars]], the grinding teeth.
The grinding teeth, related to [[same-root:mill]] through Latin [[from:molere]], to grind.
With its translations, such as Italian [[see:Molinari]] and German [[see:Müller]], among the most common surnames in many countries, since millers were always needed for bread.
Possibly the most common Italian surname, meaning [[see:miller]].
Thought to be the most common German surname, meaning [[see:miller]].

entries.term: the best thing since sliced bread
entries.note: Pre-sliced bread dates from 1928, when [[see:Otto Frederick Rohwedder]]'s automated bread slicer was first used in Chillicothe, Missouri; the machine fell apart after six months.
A jeweler from Davenport, Iowa, whose first prototype burned in 1917 before he invented the first automated bread slicer in 1928, behind [[see:the best thing since sliced bread]].
Jess's great-grandfather, inventor of agricultural tools including a basket turner, and of an early hydraulic hammer the US military used to smash roads against the Nazis.
From Greek [[from:hydraulikos organon]], water organ, a musical instrument; hydraulikos meant pertaining to a water pipe, from hydro, water, and [[from:aulos]], pipe.
Talking about galaxies always alludes to milk, just as [[see:hydraulic]] always alludes to a musical instrument.
A descendant of [[from:papyrus]]; paper itself was invented in China by the eunuch [[see:Cai Lun]], who pulped bark, hemp, rags and fishnets with water.
Not an Egyptian word but the Latin name for the reed, from Greek [[from:papyros]]; it gave [[gave:paper]], though papyrus itself isn't paper.
A Chinese [[see:eunuch]] serving the emperor who invented [[see:paper]] by pulping mulberry bark, hemp, rags and fishnets with water and drying the film.
A castrated man, castrated to pacify him so he could devote himself to protecting, in [[see:Cai Lun]]'s case, the emperor.
Made of hide, it literally means of [[from:Pergamon]], a city in modern Turkey where it supposedly replaced [[see:papyrus]]; Rob suspects [[see:parched]] influenced the spelling.
Rob assumed [[see:parchment]] came from parched, since it is dried, and suggests parched must have influenced its spelling.
First made in Han China from floating [[see:lodestone]] pointing south; the word meant a mathematical instrument that steps together, and passed to the round navigational tool.
A naturally magnetized iron stone, floated in water to point south in the first Chinese [[see:compass]]es.
A name for early Chinese [[see:compass]]es, given because their [[see:lodestone]] pointed south.
Song Dynasty name for [[see:compass]]es whose lodestones were shaped like fish, or occasionally turtles, and floated in a bowl of water to point south.
Related to the pass at the end of [[same-root:compass]].
Related to the pass at the end of [[same-root:compass]].
[[see:Johannes Gutenberg]]'s 1440s movable-type press, modelled on wine and olive oil presses, hence the name; it was first used to print [[see:indulgences]].
Invented movable type in Europe for the [[see:printing press]] to make up for a failed metal mirror business, and printed the [[see:Gutenberg Bible]].
Documents granting free passage into heaven, among the first things printed on the [[see:printing press]]; [[see:Martin Luther]]'s objection helped spark the Protestant Reformation.
Greatly objected to [[see:indulgences]], the idea that you could pay your way into heaven.
The first book printed using [[see:Johannes Gutenberg]]'s press.
Every mention of the press ultimately means pushing letters onto paper, as in the [[see:printing press]], though newspaper presses now roll rather than press.
Older than you'd think: [[see:Hero of Alexandria]] designed a coin-operated device that dispensed a fixed amount of holy water in temples.
An ancient inventor behind early [[see:vending machines]], a coin-operated holy water dispenser, and steam-driven temple [[see:automatic doors]].
A ceramic vessel from about 200 BCE holding a copper cylinder and iron rod, which some say could generate a small charge when filled with acid; its purpose is unknown.
What [[see:Alessandro Volta]]'s modern battery was called.
Inventor of the modern battery, the [[see:pile]], who gave his name to [[gave:volts]].
Named after [[from:Alessandro Volta]], inventor of the modern battery, one of a whole genre of units named after inventors.
The unit of power, one joule per second, named after [[from:James Watt]], who also invented [[see:horsepower]], a unit not named after him.
Steam engine improver who gave his name to the [[gave:watt]] and invented [[see:horsepower]] as a marketing technique.
Rob's surname, which he thinks is essentially a contraction of Watt's son.
Invented by [[see:James Watt]] as a marketing technique: his steam engine's horsepower was the number of horses it could replace.
First-century temple doors by [[see:Hero of Alexandria]] that opened when priests lit altar fires, the heat making steam that moved weights via pulleys.
Dating from the 3rd century, combining a water clock with a mechanism that dropped pebbles onto a gong at set times.
Sketched by [[see:Leonardo da Vinci]] in 1508; the first successful ones, by [[see:Adolf Fick]] in 1888, were heavy brown glass shells wearable for only a couple of hours.
Sketched concepts for [[see:contact lens]]es in 1508 but never made them.
German ophthalmologist who made the first successful [[see:contact lens]]es in 1888, testing them on rabbits; his surname is the German equivalent of a similarly spelled English word.
Flushing toilets date to about 2500 BCE in [[see:Mohenjo-Daro]], long before [[see:Thomas Crapper]], who is falsely associated with them.
An ancient city whose brick toilets connected to flowing water systems, an early example of the flushing [[see:toilet]].
A sanitation worker with patents, though none for a toilet; the story linking him to [[unrelated:crap]] and [[unrelated:crapper]] comes from his name's coincidence.
Older than the name of [[unrelated:Thomas Crapper]]; the myth arose from the coincidence of the word and a sanitation worker called Crapper.
Came later than [[see:crap]] but is unrelated to [[unrelated:Thomas Crapper]], whom nobody had heard of at the time.
A trademark coined by [[see:Charles D. Seeberger]] for an 1892 invention [[see:Jesse Wilford Reno]] called the [[see:endless conveyor elevator]]; [[see:Otis]] held the trademark.
Invented the [[see:escalator]] in 1892, first installed on Coney Island, but called it the [[see:endless conveyor elevator]].
[[see:Jesse Wilford Reno]]'s name for his invention before the word [[see:escalator]] was coined.
Coined the word [[see:escalator]].
A back-formation from [[from:escalator]], so tensions couldn't escalate before the late 1800s; Rob calls escalating tensions a journalistic cliché.
A big lift brand that bought [[see:Jesse Wilford Reno]]'s design and company and held the trademark for [[see:escalator]].
A lift brand whose name prompts Rob's pun Schindler's lift, on [[see:Schindler's List]].
A 16th-century verb for scaling fortifications with ladders, not just a Cadillac SUV, related to [[same-root:scale]] and Italian [[same-root:scala]], ladder.
To scale a cliff or wall, at the root of [[same-root:escalade]] and [[same-root:escalator]], going back to a word for ladder.
The French for a staircase; an [[see:escalator]] is basically a moving escalier.
From the 1600s, a person or muscle that lifts things, as in elevator muscles; extended in the late 1700s to machines such as grain elevators.
Unlike [[see:escalate]], not a back-formation from [[see:elevator]], which it predates by a century, though it may be one from [[from?:elevation]].
Recorded a century before [[see:elevate]], which may be a back-formation from it.
The British word for an [[see:elevator]], simpler and shorter, though no one mentions that it also lowers you.
A well-known genericized trademark, or proprietary eponym.
A well-known genericized trademark, or proprietary eponym.
One of the genericized trademarks Jess found most surprising.
A genericized trademark that surprised both hosts; in England the game also had the onomatopoeic name [[see:whiff-whaff]].
One of the genericized trademarks Jess found most surprising.
Listed by Jess as a genericized trademark.
Listed by Jess as a genericized trademark.
Listed by Jess as a genericized trademark.
Listed by Jess as a genericized trademark.
Listed by Jess as a genericized trademark.
A genericized trademark, used in a [[see:Xerox]] ad warning that misusing its name could leave its trademark wide open.
An alternative name in England for [[see:ping-pong]], admired for its onomatopoeia.
Borrowed from Moxie, a soda marketed as Moxie nerve food and named after rivers called by an Abenaki word meaning dark water.
A trademark at risk of [[see:trademark death]], so the company ran ads against using it as a verb; from [[from:xerography]], and the Russian word for photocopy.
When a brand name becomes so generic it loses its capital letter and its owner loses the trademark, also called [[see:genericide]].
Another name for [[see:trademark death]].
The older word for photocopying, with xero- from Greek for dry, since it uses dry powder melted by heat rather than wet ink; it gave [[gave:Xerox]].
A proprietary name formerly owned by [[see:Bayer]], no longer written with a capital, and the subject of a [[see:Xerox]] slogan about getting a headache.
The British word for a [[see:ballpoint pen]], from its inventor [[from:László Bíró]], whose pens the Royal Air Force bought in bulk because they worked at altitude.
Credited to [[see:László Bíró]], first to combine a ball tip with ink neither too thin nor too thick; called a [[see:Biro]] in England, [[see:birome]] in Spanish-speaking countries.
Born László Schweiger; his Jewish family took Bíró, Hungarian for judge, amid rising antisemitism; he fled via France to Argentina, where he launched the [[see:birome]].
The name [[see:László Bíró]] first gave his [[see:ballpoint pen]], developed with his brother.
The word for a [[see:ballpoint pen]] in many Spanish-speaking countries, from [[from:László Bíró]] plus the first letters of his Argentine partner's surname.
The iconic American pen brand, also used for a pen in French, from the company founded by [[from:Marcel Bich]], maker of the [[see:Cristal]].
A French baron, spelled B-I-C-H, who founded the company [[gave:Bic]] and perfected the ballpoint with the [[see:Cristal]].
[[see:Bic]]'s archetypal transparent ballpoint pen with a blue lid, one of the best-selling consumer products ever, with over a hundred billion sold.

entries.term: apparatus for facilitating the birth of a child by centrifugal force
entries.note: A 1965 patent for a spinning delivery table that flings the baby out of the birth canal into a safety net.

entries.term: apparatus for simulating a high five
entries.note: A 1994 patent for a mechanical arm on a spring-loaded pivot that slaps your palm back.
A patented battery-powered cone that rotates the ice cream so your tongue can stay put.
A patented snake leash, which Rob finds baffling since a snake is all neck.
A 1991 patent for a wristwatch counting down your approximate remaining lifespan from personal data and demographic mortality estimates.

entries.term: sanitary device to prevent male genitalia from touching the toilet water
entries.note: A patented raised stilt seat that lets the user hover above the toilet bowl.
From Latin [[from:invenire]], to come upon; first used of discovering saints' relics, as in the [[see:Invention of the Cross]], and earlier a rhetorical term for locating arguments.
A feast celebrating the 3rd-century finding of the true cross, typically credited to [[see:Saint Helena]], who found it beneath a Temple of Aphrodite in Jerusalem.
Mother of Emperor Constantine who, by some accounts, found Christ's cross in Jerusalem after a heavenly sign, the story behind the [[see:Invention of the Cross]].
From Latin, literally something invented, formed or fashioned, close to modern [[see:invention]]; in English it also came to mean myths and falsehoods, hence figments of imagination.
In Latin and Greek a device, tool or contrivance, but in 16th-century English any large structure or system, even the whole world as a constructed frame.
Originally literal: an actor dressed as a god lowered over the stage by a crane, recalling the old sense of [[see:machine]].
Now used for technology, though its essence is figurative, things that drive other things; it was shortened to [[gave:gin (machine)]], and covered in the trains, planes and automobiles episode.
Short for [[from:engine]], as in a cotton gin; used for machinery since Middle English and Old French, especially war machines and torture devices.
The drink, from a word meaning juniper, is unrelated to the machine gin short for [[unrelated:engine]], as possibly noted in the alcohol episode.
Rob suggests it fits better than [[see:invention]], since the ultimate meaning of to innovate is generating something new.
